blocks.p: A plain sale-vs-plan ratio penalises regions for shortfalls caused by lack of stock. The metric below removes the part of the gap that supply could not have covered.

rows: plan ÷ total working days × working days elapsed
clip(1 − |gap − relevant shortage| ÷ max(MTD plan, sale), 0) × 100

blocks.p: Percentages are recomputed from summed quantities at every roll-up level (article → class → region), never averaged.

blocks.code:
def plan_accuracy(plan, sale, orders, stock, days_total, days_elapsed):
    mtd = plan / days_total * days_elapsed
    supply = sale + stock
    gap = abs(mtd - sale)
    total_short = abs(orders - supply)
    rel_short = min(max(mtd - sale, 0), total_short)
    denom = max(mtd, sale)
    return round(max(0, 1 - abs(gap - rel_short) / denom) * 100) if denom else 0

projects.title: Purchase-Order Forecasting (ML experiment)
projects.tagline: Gradient-boosting ensemble for next-month PO quantity — and an honest look at why it isn't ready yet.

blocks.callout: Can ML beat the rule-based planner at predicting next month's purchase-order quantity per article? Built the full pipeline, evaluated it on a held-out month, and found that it does not yet beat a naive baseline.

Growth, consistency, PO/sales ratio, current zero-PO run, had-PO flags

blocks.p: Predictions are clipped at 0 and rounded. Each forecast gets a confidence label: HIGH if DC stock ÷ sale < 1, LOW if > 2 or no PO last month, otherwise MEDIUM.

pred = np.clip(pred, 0, None).round()

blocks.title: Ensemble + confidence

ul: Negative R² on the hold-out month means the ensemble did worse than predicting the mean — it has not beaten a naive baseline.
Article-level aggregate features were computed over all months including the test month, which leaks information and makes even this score optimistic.
With fewer than 100 articles and 5 months, the panel is too small for 88 features.
Plain K-fold CV is not time-aware; a forward-chaining split would be the correct choice.

blocks.p: Later notebook work tested which articles are predictable at all (≥ 2 PO months, min PO ≥ 10, CV < 0.4, no jump > 70%, PO last month, back-test error ≤ 20%) with a simple rule 0.6 × last + 0.3 × previous + 0.1 × trend. Only about 2% of articles passed.

ul: A complete feature-engineering and ensemble pipeline, documented and reproducible.
Clear evidence that, with current data volume, ML does not yet beat the rule-based planner — so it was not deployed.
Next: fix the leakage, use time-series CV, wait for 12+ months of history, compare against a seasonal-naive baseline.

projects.title: BTC Short-Horizon Forecasting Research
projects.tagline: Volatility ranges and gated direction models on 1-second data, with leakage tests and fee-aware walk-forward backtests.

blocks.callout: Question: can short-horizon BTC moves be forecast well enough to trade after fees? Answer, after a leakage-safe study: ranges yes (well calibrated), direction barely, profit no.

kv: Public exchange archive: spot BTC/USDT 1-second bars + perpetual futures 1-minute bars, ~184 days; live recorder
Main model 20 minutes, decision every minute; short-horizon study 10 s – 20 min
All written by hand in NumPy: ridge, Newton logistic, MLP, 1D-CNN, AdamW

rows: Archive files verified by SHA-256, up to 4 retries with backoff
Price, volume, buyer-initiated volume, trade count
After a gap > 30 s, the next 24 h are masked as unreliable
Recorder back-fills 30 h at start, optional order-book snapshots

Log realised variance over 5 min, 20 min, 1 h, 4 h, 24 h (from 10-s returns); volume and trade count 5 min vs 24 h; jump share from bipower variation; |order-flow imbalance| 5 min; half-hour × weekend seasonality
Order-flow imbalance 1/5/15 min and 1 h; vol-scaled returns 1/5/20 min, 1 h, 4 h; gap to 1-h VWAP; perp–spot basis deviation; perp lead 5 min; perp flow 5/15 min
Last 30 one-minute returns and flow imbalances
Ridge regression on log forward 20-min realised variance
Filtered historical simulation: quantiles of returns ÷ predicted vol on a 14-day calibration slice
Ridge logistic regression (Newton steps) + Platt calibration
Range shifted so P(return > 0) equals the stated probability
Wide-and-deep MLP 128-64-32, ReLU, dropout 10%, AdamW; last layer zero-initialised so it starts at the linear model; 3-seed average
Direction used only if log-loss gain vs base rate has one-sided t p < 0.0228 (daily means, Newey-West) and Platt slope > 0

blocks.code:
for fold in walk_forward(train=60d, cal=14d, test=7d, purge=21min):
    vol = ridge(Xv[fit], log_fwd_var[fit], lam=1e-3)
    dir_ = ridge_logistic(Xd[fit], up[fit], lam=0.25)
    z = ret[cal] / exp(0.5 * vol(Xv[cal]))
    zq = quantiles(z, grid)
    t, days = newey_west_t(logloss(base) - logloss(dir_(cal)))
    gate = pvalue(t, days) < 0.0228 and platt_slope > 0
    p = clip(platt(dir_(test)) if gate else base, 0.40, 0.60)
    q = sigma(test) * (interp(TAUS, grid, zq) - interp(1 - p, grid, zq))
blocks.title: Walk-forward fold

ul: Walk-forward: 60-day window (incl. 14-day calibration), 7-day test step, 21-minute purge between fit, calibration and test.
All settings fixed before testing; significance on daily means.
Baselines: unconditional, last-1h volatility, last-1h volatility with clock adjustment.
Placebo: labels rolled by ≥ 2 days.
Automatic red flags: AUC > 0.56, accuracy > 0.54, vol R² > 0.8, probability spread > 0.05, 90% coverage off by > 3 pts, < 120 days.
Paper rules: trade at p ≥ 0.55 / ≤ 0.45, target 1.5σ, trailing stop 1.0σ, 20-min time exit, 0.1% fee per side, 50 coin-flip baselines.

rows: Truncate the future, features must be identical
Implied P(up) matches, quantiles don't cross, save/load round-trip

blocks.p: AR(1) volatility process with a clock pattern. No planted signal: AUC 0.5013, gate on in 0 of 5 folds. Planted edge: AUC 0.5518, beating 20 of 20 placebo runs — the pipeline finds signal only when it exists.

rows: Gate on in 6 of 18 folds; final gain p = 0.358 (not significant)

ul: Most confident 1% at 10 s: 81.1%; acting 2 s late drops 10-s accuracy to 55.4%; placebo ≈ 50% at every horizon.
Range trading (1D-CNN on 15-min candles): 71.2% vs 71.7% random-walk baseline — no skill; −12.8% after fees.
Live engine matched tested forecasts in 720 of 720 replays.

blocks.callout: Conclusion: volatility ranges are forecastable and well calibrated; direction carries a small, real but untradable signal — fees are larger than the typical move. Reported as a negative result rather than tuned into a false positive.
